![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14036389/assets/f725b571954587b7b88426a254d7a6fc05f09b63ab2cc94b81303a510e8c1798.png)

The graph of $y=f(x),$ shown above, consists of two line segments. Find the value of ${\int }_{-2}^{3}f(x)\,\text{d}x.$
questions.worked_solution:
We divide the interval of integration into $3$ regions: the line segment for $x\in [-2,0],$ the line segment for $x\in [0,2),$ and the line segment for $x\in [2,3].$ Therefore, we can write the required integral as follows:

$$
{\int }_{-2}^{3}f(x)\,\text{d}x={{{\int }_{-2}^{0}f(x)\,\text{d}x}_{⏟}}_{{A}_{1}}+{{{\int }_{0}^{2}f(x)\,\text{d}x}_{⏟}}_{-{A}_{2}}+{{{\int }_{2}^{3}f(x)\,\text{d}x}_{⏟}}_{{A}_{3}}
$$

- The $1$st integral represents the signed area between the curve and the $x$-axis, where $x\in [-2,0].$ The corresponding region is a right triangle, so we find the area using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{1} & =\frac{1}{2}(bh) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(2\cdot 2) \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

- The $2$nd integral represents the signed area between the curve and the $x$-axis, where $x\in [0,2).$ The corresponding region is a right triangle, so we find the area using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{2} & =\frac{1}{2}(bh) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(2\cdot 2) \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the region lies below the $x$-axis, we have

$$
{\int }_{0}^{2}f(x)\,\text{d}x=-{A}_{2}=-2.
$$

- The $3$rd integral represents the signed area between the curve and the $x$-axis, where $x\in [2,3].$ The corresponding region is a rectangle, so we find the area using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{3} & =bh \\  & =1\cdot 2 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-2}^{3}f(x)\,\text{d}x & ={A}_{1}-{A}_{2}+{A}_{3} \\  & =2-2+2 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

The graph of $y=f(x),$ shown above, consists of two line segments. Find the value of ${\int }_{-3}^{4}f(x)\,\text{d}x.$
questions.worked_solution:
The graph consists of two parts: the line segment for $x\in [-3,0]$ and the line segment for $x\in (0,4].$ Therefore, we can write the required integral as follows:

$$
{\int }_{-3}^{4}f(x)\,\text{d}x={{{\int }_{-3}^{0}f(x)\,\text{d}x}_{⏟}}_{{A}_{1}}+{{{\int }_{0}^{4}f(x)\,\text{d}x}_{⏟}}_{-{A}_{2}}
$$

- The $1$st integral represents the signed area between the curve and the $x$-axis, where $x\in [-3,0].$ The corresponding region is a triangle, so we find the area using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{1} & =\frac{1}{2}bh \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 3\cdot 3 \\  & =4.5.\end{aligned}
$$

- The $2$nd integral represents the signed area between the curve and the $x$-axis, where $x\in (0,4].$ The corresponding region is a rectangle, so we find the area using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{2} & =ab \\  & =2\cdot 4 \\  & =8.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the region lies below the $x$-axis, we have

$$
{\int }_{0}^{4}f(x)\,\text{d}x=-{A}_{2}=-8.
$$

Finally, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-3}^{4}f(x)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{-3}^{0}f(x)\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{4}f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =4.5-8 \\  & =-3.5.\end{aligned}
$$

- The $1$st integral represents the signed area between the curve and the $x$-axis, where $x\in [-4,0].$ The corresponding region is a trapezoid, so we find the area using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{1} & =\frac{1}{2}(a+b)h \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(1+3)(4) \\  & =8.\end{aligned}

$$

- The $3$rd integral represents the signed area between the curve and the $x$-axis, where $x\in [4,6].$ The corresponding region is a right triangle, so we find the area using the formula

$$

The graph of $y=f(x),$ shown above, consists of four line segments. Find the value of ${\int }_{-3}^{3}f(x)\,\text{d}x.$
questions.worked_solution:
The graph consists of four parts: the line segment for $x\in [-3,-2),$ the line segment for $x\in [-2,-1),$ the line segment for $x\in [-1,1),$ and the line segments for $x\in [1,3].$ Therefore, we can write the required integral as follows:

$$
{\int }_{-3}^{3}f(x)\,\text{d}x={{{\int }_{-3}^{-2}f(x)\,\text{d}x}_{⏟}}_{{A}_{1}}+{{{\int }_{-2}^{-1}f(x)\,\text{d}x}_{⏟}}_{-{A}_{2}}+{{{\int }_{-1}^{1}f(x)\,\text{d}x}_{⏟}}_{{A}_{3}}+{{{\int }_{1}^{3}f(x)\,\text{d}x}_{⏟}}_{-{A}_{4}}
$$

- The $1$st integral represents the signed area between the curve and the $x$-axis, where $x\in [-3,-2).$ The corresponding region is a triangle, so we find the area using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{1} & =\frac{1}{2}bh \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 1\cdot 2 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

- The $2$nd integral represents the signed area between the curve and the $x$-axis, where $x\in [-2,-1).$ The corresponding region is a triangle, so we find the area using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{2} & =\frac{1}{2}bh \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 1\cdot 2 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the region lies below the $x$-axis, we have 

$$
{\int }_{-2}^{-1}f(x)\,\text{d}x=-{A}_{2}=-1.
$$

- The $3$rd integral represents the signed area between the curve and the $x$-axis, where $x\in [-1,1).$ The corresponding region is a triangle, so we find the area using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{3} & =\frac{1}{2}bh \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 2\cdot 2 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

- The $4$th integral represents the signed area between the curve and the $x$-axis, where $x\in [1,3].$ The corresponding region is a triangle, so we find the area using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{4} & =\frac{1}{2}bh \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 2\cdot 2 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the region lies below the $x$-axis, we have 

$$
{\int }_{1}^{3}f(x)\,\text{d}x=-{A}_{4}=-2.
$$

Finally, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-3}^{3}f(x)\,\text{d}x & ={A}_{1}-{A}_{2}+{A}_{3}-{A}_{4} \\  & =1-1+2-2 \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The graph consists of $2$ parts: the line segment for $x\in [-2,2)$ and the arc of the semi-circle for $x\in [2,6].$ So, we can use the additive property of integrals to get

$$
{\int }_{-2}^{6}f(x)\,\text{d}x={{{\int }_{-2}^{2}f(x)\,\text{d}x}_{⏟}}_{{A}_{1}}+{{{\int }_{2}^{6}f(x)\,\text{d}x}_{⏟}}_{{A}_{2}}.
$$

- The $1$st integral represents the signed area between the curve and the $x$-axis, where $x\in [-2,2).$ The corresponding region is a triangle, so we find the area using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{1} & =\frac{1}{2}b\cdot h \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(4)\cdot 4 \\  & =8.\end{aligned}
$$

- The $2$nd integral represents the signed area between the curve and the $x$-axis, where $x\in [2,6].$ The corresponding region is a semi-circle, so we find the area using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{2} & =\frac{1}{2}\pi {r}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\pi \cdot (2)^{2} \\  & =2\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-2}^{6}f(x)\,\text{d}x & ={A}_{1}+{A}_{2} \\  & =8+2\pi .\end{aligned}

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14036389/assets/ad45cbdcd126df931f1a35c60ca12b45d520a2a0a5cddf4fa012c0515d3024c7.png)

The graph of $y=f(x),$ shown above, consists of two line segments. Find the value of $\displaystyle \int_{0}^{4} f(x)\: \textrm{d}x.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The graph consists of two parts: the line segment for $x \in [0,2)$ and the line segment for $x \in [2,4].$ Therefore, we can write the required integral as follows:

$$
\int_{0}^{4} f(x)\: \textrm{d}x = \underbrace{\int_{0}^{2} f(x)\: \textrm{d}x}_{A_1} + \underbrace{\int_{2}^{4} f(x)\: \textrm{d}x}_{-A_2}.
$$

- The $1$st integral represents the signed area between the curve and the $x$-axis, where $x \in [0,2).$ The corresponding region is a rectangle, so we find the area using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{1} & =bh \\  & =2\cdot 2 \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

- The $2$nd integral represents the signed area between the curve and the $x$-axis, where $x \in [2,4].$ The corresponding region is a right triangle, so we find the area using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{2} & =\frac{1}{2}bh \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 2\cdot 2 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the region lies below the $x$-axis, we have 

$$
\int_{2}^{4} f(x)\: \textrm{d}x =-A_2 = -2.
$$

Finally, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{4}f(x)\,\text{d}x & ={A}_{1}-{A}_{2} \\  & =4-2 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Calculating the Definite Integral of a Piecewise Curved Function Given Its Graph
canonical_examples.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14036389/assets/36c6a1c84e0b0c32a5fd35fd422645f60340da6d205dd8cc31054cd558c2f5f9.png)

Given the graph of $y=f(x)$ above, find the value of $\displaystyle \int_{-4}^4 f(x) \,\textrm{d}x.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The graph consists of four parts: the arc of a semi-circle for $x\in [-4,0],$ a line segment for $x\in (0,2),$ a line segment for $x\in (2,4],$ and the point at $x=2.$ So, we can use the additive property of integrals to get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-4}^{4}f(x)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{-4}^{0}f(x)\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{2}f(x)\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{2}^{2}f(x)\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{2}^{4}f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={{{\int }_{-4}^{0}f(x)\,\text{d}x}_{⏟}}_{{A}_{1}}+{{{\int }_{0}^{2}f(x)\,\text{d}x}_{⏟}}_{-{A}_{2}}+0+{{{\int }_{2}^{4}f(x)\,\text{d}x}_{⏟}}_{{A}_{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

- The $1$st integral represents the signed area between the curve and the $x$-axis, where $x \in [-4,0].$ The corresponding region is a semi-circle with a radius of $2,$ so we find the area using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{1} & =\frac{1}{2}\pi {r}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \pi \cdot {2}^{2} \\  & =2\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

- The $2$nd integral represents the signed area between the curve and the $x$-axis, where $x \in (0,2).$ The corresponding region is a right triangle, so we find the area using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{2} & =\frac{1}{2}bh \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 2\cdot 2 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the region lies below the $x$-axis, we have

$$
\int_{0}^{2} f(x)\: \textrm{d}x = -A_2 = -2.
$$

- The $3$rd integral represents the signed area between the curve and the $x$-axis, where $x \in (2,4].$  The corresponding region is a right triangle, so we find the area using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{3} & =\frac{1}{2}bh \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 2\cdot 2 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-4}^{4}f(x)\,\text{d}x & ={A}_{1}-{A}_{2}+{A}_{3} \\  & =2\pi -2+2 \\  & =2\pi .\end{aligned}
$$
